aiOverview.content: As of March and April 2026, COVID-19 continues to circulate, with new, highly mutated Omicron subvariants—notably the BA.3.2 "Cicada" variant—serving as a major driver of cases in the U.S. and globally. Symptoms in 2026 have evolved to be very similar to other circulating respiratory infections, such as the flu, RSV, and the common cold. Common 2026 COVID-19 Symptoms The 2026 variants generally produce mild to moderate symptoms that often start in the upper respiratory tract. Common symptoms include: Severe or "Razorblade" Sore Throat: A distinct, sharp, or intensely painful sore throat. Persistent Cough: Usually a dry, hacking cough. Runny or Stuffy Nose: Significant nasal congestion. Fatigue and Muscle Aches: Lingering tiredness and body aches. Headache: Frequently reported symptom. Fever or Chills: These are still common, though sometimes milder than in earlier years. Sneezing: Common in the 2026 variant, often making it hard to distinguish from a cold. Distinguishing Features in 2026 "Cicada" Variant (BA.3.2): This variant is characterized by its ability to evade immune protection due to high mutations in the spike protein. It is highly contagious. "Stratus" Variant: Another sub-variant spreading in 2026, often causing "scratchy" or raspy voices, similar to "razor throat". Loss of Taste/Smell: While still a possible symptom, it is reported less frequently than in early pandemic years, but remains a strong indicator if present. "Long COVID" Trends (March 2026): Research continues to show that long-term symptoms (Long COVID) can persist for over 2.5 years, with common long-term effects including severe dyspnea (shortness of breath), cognitive dysfunction ("brain fog"), and profound fatigue. When to Seek Emergency Care If you or a loved one experience any of the following, seek immediate medical attention: Difficulty breathing or severe shortness of breath. Persistent chest pain or pressure. Confusion or inability to wake up. Bluish lips or face. Note: Because COVID symptoms in 2026 are often indistinguishable from the flu or a cold, testing is the only definitive way to know if you have COVID-19.
